claims.text: As-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type high-entropy alloys contain nanoscale variations in local chemical ordering and strain.
Local chemical-order and strain variations create regions with different magnetic exchange strengths.
The spatially varying exchange strengths dictate a sharp, first-order magnetostructural transition.
Nanoscale chemical and strain inhomogeneity causes pronounced hysteresis during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
Reducing nanoscale heterogeneity by controlled annealing will make the magnetocaloric response more gradual and reversible.
The as-deposited material is a thin film or coating with a single ordered phase.
Annealing well below the order-disorder transition can homogenize local chemical ordering without causing grain growth.
Local chemical ordering modulates magnetic exchange interactions.
Local strain modulates magnetic exchange interactions.
Variations in local ordering and strain control magnetic domain-wall pinning.
As-deposited inhomogeneity creates local energy barriers responsible for a sharp, hysteretic magnetostructural transition.
Mild annealing relaxes strain gradients and homogenizes chemical order.
Relaxing strain gradients and homogenizing chemical order reduce domain-wall pinning.
Reduced domain-wall pinning smooths the magnetostructural transition and lowers hysteresis.
The annealed alloy should exhibit a broader and less hysteretic magnetocaloric entropy-change curve than the as-deposited alloy.
Annealing should preserve a similar magnitude of magnetocaloric entropy change.
The annealed alloy should have lower energy loss during low-field magnetic cycling.
The proposed behavior is limited to rapidly deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type alloys that retain nanoscale inhomogeneity and may fail in multiphase regimes or at substantially higher applied fields.
A failure to obtain both a greater-than-20% reduction in hysteresis-loop area and a broader, smoother entropy-change curve is specified as the falsifying result.
